sections.h2: What does an Indiana quitclaim deed actually transfer?
sections.html:
An Indiana quitclaim deed passes whatever interest the grantor has and nothing beyond it. IC 32-17-2-2 says a quitclaim conveys "all the estate that the grantor may convey by a deed of bargain and sale," so the grantee's rights are only as good as the grantor's.

The statute also supplies a short form. Under IC 32-21-1-15, a conveyance worded in substance as "A.B. quitclaims to C.D." is valid when it describes the property, states the consideration after "for the sum of," and is signed, sealed and acknowledged. A deed in that shape is a good quitclaim to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns.

What the form leaves out is any promise about title. A buyer who takes a quitclaim has no deed covenants to fall back on. That gap matters most when a buyer is paying money for the property.

sections.h2: What must an Indiana quitclaim deed include to be recorded?
sections.html:
The deed needs a notarial act, two mailing addresses, a preparer statement and a Social Security redaction affirmation, in addition to the grantor's signature. Each requirement traces to a section of the code.

  • Acknowledgment or proof. IC 32-21-2-3 requires a notarial officer's acknowledgment or a proof, and Indiana allows remote notarization under the cited sections.
  • Addresses. The conveyance must state the mailing address for tax statements and the grantee's mailing address. The grantee's address has to be a street address or rural route address, and the statement goes at the end of the deed next to the preparer statements.
  • Prepared by. Under IC 36-2-11-15, the preparer's name must be printed, typed, stamped or signed at the end, for example "This instrument was prepared by" and the name.
  • Redaction. The preparer affirms under penalties of perjury that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers, unless a law requires them.
  • Names. Each signer's name is printed under the signature and kept identical throughout, including the notary block.
  • Format. Margins are at least 2 inches top and bottom on the first and last pages, paper is white and no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, and bound or continuous-form pages are not accepted.

A deed signed outside Indiana is treated differently on one point: instruments executed or acknowledged outside the state are exempt from the preparer statement rule, and a document in a foreign language needs an English translation.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Indiana?
sections.html:
The base county recorder fee for an ordinary deed is $25 under IC 36-2-7-10, and the sales disclosure filing adds $20 when it applies. The table lists the fees found in the code and in DLGF materials. Counties may add small charges by ordinance, so the recorder's current schedule controls.

ItemAmountWhere it comes from
Recording a deed (standard pages)$25 flatIC 36-2-7-10
Oversized pages (over 8.5 by 14 inches)$25 first page, $5 each additionalIC 36-2-7-10
Copy of a recorded page$1 per page up to 11 by 17 inchesIC 36-2-7-10
Certifying a document$5IC 36-2-7-10
Sales disclosure form fee$20, paid to the county auditorDLGF presentation
Affordable housing fund (some counties)$10 per documentIC 36-2-7-10

Anyone budgeting for a family transfer should also ask the county auditor whether the endorsement carries a charge, and should expect a notary fee on top.

sections.h2: Does a quitclaim deed need an auditor endorsement and a sales disclosure form?
sections.html:
Most Indiana deeds pass through the county auditor before the recorder, and many transfers also need a sales disclosure form. The recorder can record a land conveyance only if the auditor has endorsed it "duly entered for taxation subject to final acceptance for transfer," "not taxable," or "duly entered for taxation," as IC 36-2-11-14 puts it.

The sales disclosure rules are narrower. DLGF's presentation says a form is required whenever a real property interest moves for valuable consideration in a deed, contract, judgment or similar document. Exempt from the form altogether are quitclaim deeds that do not serve as a source of title, gifts with no valuable consideration, mortgages, and transfers to a government unit. Foreclosure, divorce, court-ordered, condemnation and probate transfers need the form but owe no fee.

The form must be signed by the transferor and the transferee, reviewed and stamped by the county assessor, and then forwarded to the auditor. The auditor may not accept a conveyance when the form is missing, incomplete or unstamped. Each parcel needs its own form, although one form can cover contiguous parcels in the same taxing district under a single deed.

sections.h2: When does a quitclaim deed make sense, and when does it cause trouble?
sections.html:
A quitclaim fits transfers between people who already know the property's history, such as moving a house into a spouse's name or a family member's name. It is a weaker fit for a sale to a stranger, because the grantor gives no assurance of clean title.

Situations that tend to go wrong include:

  • A deed from someone who does not hold full title, which passes only the partial interest the grantor really has.
  • Using a quitclaim to pass an inherited house before anyone has opened an estate. A personal representative's deed under IC 29-1-7.5-3.6 is the statutory way to convey title out of an estate.
  • A deed that skips the auditor's endorsement, the sales disclosure form or the grantee's street address. The recorder may refuse it, and Monroe County says it does not accept P.O. boxes.

A quitclaim cannot create ownership the grantor never had, so the grantor's own deed in the county records is worth reading before anyone signs.

sections.h2: How does a transfer on death deed compare with a quitclaim?
sections.html:
A transfer on death deed names who gets the house after the owner dies, and it has different rules from a present-day quitclaim. IC 32-17-14-11 requires recording with the county recorder before the owner dies, needs no consideration or delivery, and does not require the auditor's endorsement.

The ownership form matters here too. A deed on tenancy by the entirety property is void unless the other spouse joins, and a joint tenancy with survivorship is severed into a tenancy in common. Under IC 32-21-1-15(b), once a transfer on death deed is recorded, a later conveyance of the same property is void unless it was recorded before the owner's death. A homeowner who later wants to sell should check the county records first.

sections.h2: What if the property is in a tax sale redemption period?
sections.html:
An owner who deeds a house during a tax sale redemption period faces a special rule. Under IC 32-21-8-7, the auditor cannot endorse the conveyance until the buyer has paid the county treasurer the full redemption amount under IC 6-1.1-25 and shown written proof. The conveyance is also void unless it is recorded with the recorder by the end of the redemption period.

A quitclaim in that situation does not shortcut the redemption. The treasurer's payoff, the auditor's endorsement and the recorder's filing all have to happen in order, and the one-year redemption period for ordinary tax sales runs on its own clock.

sections.h2: Selling a house after a quitclaim transfer in Indiana
sections.html:
A cash buyer still needs the chain of title to hold together, so a recent quitclaim among family members raises questions a title company will ask. Who signed, whether all owners joined, whether the deed was recorded, and whether a sales disclosure form went in with it are the points that decide how fast a closing moves.

Recent quitclaims also affect property tax benefits. The homestead deduction is tied to the owner's principal residence, and the 2026 rules add a 10 percent penalty for keeping a deduction after ineligibility. An owner who stops living in a house after deeding it should notify the county auditor.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed legal in Indiana?
faqs.a: Yes. IC 32-21-1-15 recognizes a conveyance worded in substance as "A.B. quitclaims to C.D." if it describes the property, states the consideration, and is signed, sealed and acknowledged.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Indiana?
faqs.a: The recorder charges $25 for an ordinary deed under IC 36-2-7-10, with a $25 plus $5 per extra page schedule for oversized pages. A sales disclosure form adds a $20 fee paid to the county auditor when the transfer is for value.

faqs.q: Does Indiana require a notary on a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Yes. IC 32-21-2-3 requires an acknowledgment or a proof, and Indiana allows a remote notary under the cited statutes.

faqs.q: Do I need a sales disclosure form for a quitclaim deed in Indiana?
faqs.a: Not always. DLGF lists quitclaim deeds that do not serve as a source of title, and gifts with no valuable consideration, among the transfers that do not need the form. A transfer for valuable consideration does need one.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?
faqs.a: No. It passes only the interest the grantor has under IC 32-17-2-2, and the short statutory form contains no title promises.

faqs.q: Can a quitclaim be used to transfer a house after death?
faqs.a: Only the owner can sign while alive. After death, a personal representative conveys with a representative's deed, or a transfer on death deed recorded before death takes effect under IC 32-17-14-11.
